newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Faulding upbeat on U.S. business.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Faulding upbeat on U.S. business.

text.p: Australian pharmaceuticals manufacturer F.H. Faulding and Co Ltd said on Wednesday it expected to finalise the US$70 million mop up of its U.S. subsidiary Faulding Inc by about late September.

Faulding managing director Ed Tweddell told Reuters in an interview the company had yet to decide how much it would raise from a rights issue to fund the deal, but it believed the move underlined the company's confidence in its growth prospects.

"We have not yet actually come up with anything in the way of detail (about the issue) yet," he said. He said a board meeting earlier in the day had set up an independent committee of Faulding Inc's non-aligned directors to assess the bid.

Faulding on Tuesday said it would offer US$12 a share for the 38 percent or 5.2 million shares it did not already own in Faulding Inc, which posted a small net profit in the last quarter to turn around the difficulties of recent years.

"We believe the offer is fair to both the F.H Faulding shareholders and the Faulding Inc minorities," Tweddell said, adding the price was a 78 percent premium on the stock's value a year ago. He said he expected the bid to succeed, although it would not be a major setback if it did not.
With the move, the company was signalling its belief that investing in its own business was "a pretty good investment for our own shareholders," he said.
"I see the Faulding Inc merger as being an extension of that confidence," he said.

While Faulding currently had no specific plans for major capital investment in the U.S. arm, it saw the business as a significant growth area and would prefer to put investment funds into a wholly owned subsidiary, he said.

Tweddell said Faulding had the internal resources to fund the bid and had considered other funding options, but it believed the rights issue allowed shareholders to participate in an important part of the company's development.

"We really have got our act together in the drug development side of the business over the last year or so, not only in the U.S. but throughout the group and that underpins our basic confidence in the future of the Faulding group."
Faulding's product development and registration history had grown "astronomically" in Europe over the last few years.
"There is a conscious effort that, as we expand our geography, we grow our business organically by making sure we have the products approved to move into these markets," he said.

Tweddell was also upbeat about the company's proposed joint venture with U.S. healthcare company Cardinal Health Inc for the Australian distribution of Cardinal's automated hospital pharmacy dispensary and information systems.
He said Faulding believed there was "a huge pent-up demand" for such systems in Australian public and private hospitals, driven by the need for greater efficiencies and cost savings.

Tweddell said the company expected the joint venture - with its business plan hoped to be finalised next week - to be significantly profitable over five years and was part of its strategy to boost its consumer health business.
Tweddell said the venture offered opportunities for the two companies to combine on other services and in other regions.
"Obviously we are forming an important relationship with Cardinal ... and part of the attraction of this relationship is hopefully the potential to do other things," he said.
Faulding shares were down 29 cents at A$7.55 (US$5.74) in early afternoon trading, valuing the company at A$959 million.

Faulding reported a net profit of A$16.21 million for the six months to December 31, up from A$12.40 million a year earlier. Net profit in the year to June 30 was A$28 million on sales of A$1.54 billion.
